planting.note: Divide basal offsets or plant container-grown specimens after frost into rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; selloum's roots survive brief light frost in zone 9 even when top growth is damaged, resprouting from the crown.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; selloum is a bold, trunk-forming tropical aroid with massive, deeply and irregularly lobed leaves on long petioles that arch outward from a stout central stem, eventually developing a short, thick, above-ground trunk covered in old leaf-base scars as it ages. It is one of the most widely planted tropical foliage specimens in warm-climate landscapes, valued for filling large shaded areas with bold, architectural texture and requiring relatively little maintenance beyond removing old, yellowing lower leaves. Established plants tolerate brief light frost, with damaged foliage resprouting readily from the crown in spring even after a hard freeze kills the top growth back in zone 9. Provide ample room to spread, since a mature specimen can reach 6 feet or more in height and equal spread, and keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged during the growing season.

planting.note: Divide basal offsets or plant container-grown specimens after frost into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Xanadu forms a tidy, non-vining, self-heading clump considerably more compact than its parent, selloum.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Xanadu is a compact, self-heading philodendron hybrid selected for its neat, rounded mound of deeply lobed, glossy dark green leaves that never develop the sprawling scale or trunk of full-sized selloum, making it far better suited to foundation plantings, mixed shade borders, and mass plantings in smaller garden spaces. It holds a tidy, symmetrical form with minimal care, needing only the occasional removal of an old lower leaf to stay attractive year-round in frost-free climates. Container culture works well anywhere, with plants moved indoors to a bright spot before the first frost in climates colder than its hardiness range. Established outdoor plantings tolerate brief light frost with foliage damage but generally recover from the crown, much like other tender aroids grown in zone 9.

planting.note: Divide offset pups or plant container-grown specimens in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; blood banana is grown for its striking foliage rather than for edible fruit, which is small and full of hard seeds.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; blood banana is an ornamental selection of the wild seed banana grown for its dramatic broad, blue-green leaves heavily splashed and streaked with maroon-red blotches, with pseudostems that carry the same deep burgundy mottling. It is smaller and more manageable than fruiting dessert bananas, reaching 5 to 8 feet, making it a good fit for mixed tropical borders and large containers where a full-sized banana would overwhelm the space. Small, seedy, essentially inedible fruit may form after flowering, so grow it strictly as a bold foliage and texture plant rather than for any edible crop. In zone 9 the top growth is killed by frost most winters, but a thick mulch over the root zone helps the rhizome resprout vigorously once the soil warms in spring; where winters are colder, dig and store rhizomes indoors or grow in a large container that can be moved under cover.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cotton needs a long, hot, essentially frost-free growing season of five to six months to fully mature and open its bolls.

directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has thoroughly warmed; upland cotton is the classic Southern row crop, grown by home gardeners today mostly as a novelty, dried-arrangement, or heirloom fiber crop rather than for commercial-scale harvest. Showy, pale yellow to cream flowers resembling a hibiscus bloom (a close botanical relative) open over midsummer and fade to pink before dropping, revealing a green boll that swells over several weeks and eventually splits open to expose the fluffy white — or, in naturally colored heirloom varieties, tan, green, or brown — lint prized by spinners and fiber crafters. Because it needs a long, hot, frost-free season to fully open its bolls, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed as early as safely possible after last frost and choose an early-maturing variety. Watch for cotton's classic pest pressures, including boll weevil and aphids, and rotate planting location yearly to reduce soil-borne disease buildup.
sources: USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Direct sow 4 weeks before last frost, or in early fall in mild-winter climates, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; black mustard bolts and sets seed quickly once summer heat arrives, so aim for a full life cycle in cool weather.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in early fall where winters are mild; black mustard grows quickly into a tall, branching plant with small, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers in loose clusters, followed by slender seed pods that shatter readily when fully ripe. It produces the pungent, sharply flavored small brown-black seeds traditionally used to make true Dijon-style prepared mustard and are also used whole in Indian and other South Asian tempering and pickling, delivering more heat and complexity than the milder white mustard seed. Because ripe pods shatter and drop seed the moment they dry, harvest whole seed heads into a paper bag as soon as pods begin to turn from green to brown, then finish drying and threshing indoors to avoid losing the crop to shattering in the field. Rotate away from other brassica family crops each season to reduce pest and disease buildup, and expect volunteer seedlings the following year from any seed that drops before harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; canary grass tolerates light frost as a seedling and is grown as a quick-maturing cool-season grain and cover.

directions: Broadcast or drill seed into average, well-drained soil in full sun as soon as the ground can be worked in early spring; canary grass is a fast, upright cool-season cereal grass grown for its small, shiny, oil-rich seed, the same 'canary seed' used commercially in birdseed mixes and increasingly grown as a human food-grade gluten-free grain. Dense, cylindrical, spike-like seed heads form atop the narrow foliage in early summer and dry to a pale straw color when ready to harvest, at which point stands can be cut and threshed like a small grain of wheat or oats. It matures quickly enough to fit into a short cool-season window, tolerating late spring frost far better than warm-season grain crops, and also serves as an effective erosion-control and quick-cover companion in a grain rotation. Harvest promptly once heads dry, since shattering losses increase the longer mature stands stand in the field.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
USDA ARS National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN-Global)
